analysis.one_liner: Lets any American buy into Medicare coverage by paying age-based premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and its Health Subcommittee until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend Medicare law to let any U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident enroll in Medicare and pay monthly premiums for it, instead of relying on employer plans or private individual-market insurance. It never moved: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and no action followed before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone without Medicare — especially people who find private insurance expensive or unreliable — could buy a government-run Medicare plan at premiums set from the actual costs of their age group. People under 65, who today cannot buy Medicare, gain a guaranteed public alternative. Medicare itself would gain a pool of premium-paying enrollees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone wanting to buy Medicare coverage

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident not already in Medicare would be eligible to enroll in the program's insurance coverage.

Enrollees would pay monthly premiums, with rates calculated from costs within their own age cohort — under 19, 19-25, 26-35, 36-45, 46-55, and 56-64 — rather than from the costs of the 65-and-over population.
Coverage could not begin before the first calendar year after enactment, giving agencies and providers time to set up enrollment.
The buy-in would be voluntary; nobody would be required to leave an existing plan.

analysis.who_pays: Enrollees would pay premiums sized to their age group's expected costs, so premiums for older buyers could be substantial. Private health insurers would lose customers who choose Medicare instead. If premiums were set too low, taxpayers would ultimately backstop Medicare's shortfalls.

drawbacks.text: Premiums are set by age-cohort costs, so an older buyer between jobs could face a very high monthly bill — the bill offers no subsidies to help people pay them.
Voluntary buy-ins can attract disproportionately sick enrollees, which can push premiums higher than the government's cost estimates assume; taxpayers stand behind Medicare's balance sheet.
Private insurers and some providers argue a cheaper public plan can draw patients away from private networks and shift costs; the bill does not address those transition effects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The buy-in would give the uninsured and unhappily insured a genuine public alternative priced at cost, with no new taxes and no mandate. The real limits are design ones: no subsidies mean older and lower-income buyers may find the age-priced premiums unaffordable, and the risk of adverse selection falls on Medicare. On balance it is a straightforward expansion of a public program rather than a costly new entitlement.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and neither ever held a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the bill on February 5, 2013.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel with jurisdiction over Medicare financing.
On February 14, 2013, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill's last recorded action is that subcommittee referral, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, who kept the under-65 insurance market to themselves with no public competitor, and the Ways and Means Committee's leadership, who faced no record vote on the idea.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

for.name: 1 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 14, 2013 and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored and a single Democrat cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee let it sit without a hearing.

industries.note: A Medicare buy-in gives individuals a government-run alternative to private individual and employer plans, letting them exit those markets. Insurers' interest in blocking the bill runs against the option it would give consumers.

industries.industry: Medicare program (and the taxpayers behind it)
industries.note: Medicare would gain premium-paying enrollees and a broader pool, but a voluntary buy-in can concentrate sicker enrollees and leave taxpayers exposed if premiums are underpriced.
